title: AI forecasts differ mainly over economic consequences and produce distinct policy preferences across expert and public groups
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35046 survey of five groups forecasting the economic effects of AI
geography: United States; forecasts and policy preferences from academic economists, AI-company employees, AI policy researchers, highly accurate forecasters, and the general public

observations.period: 2026; forecasts elicited across five respondent groups

denominator.unit: respondent groups compared in the forecasting study

near_term_ai_expectation.value: the median respondent in each group expects substantial advances in AI capabilities by 2030

baseline_growth_expectation.value: 2.5% annual GDP growth expected by the median respondent, above typical medium-run 2.0% and long-run 1.7% government/private forecasts

rapid_progress_growth.value: around 4% annualized GDP growth under a rapid-AI-progress scenario

rapid_progress_labor_force.value: labor-force participation forecast to fall from 62% currently to 55% by 2050, with roughly half the decline attributed to AI and equivalent to about 10 million lost jobs

disagreement_source.value: expert disagreement is driven primarily by beliefs about the economic effects of highly capable AI rather than disagreement about the pace of AI progress

policy_preference_split.value: experts strongly favor targeted worker retraining, while the general public supports targeted programs plus broader interventions including a job guarantee and universal basic income

observations.method: Survey-based elicitation of forecasts and policy preferences across five respondent groups, with a variance decomposition of disagreement and conditional rapid-progress scenario analysis.
observations.uncertainty: These are beliefs and conditional forecasts, not observed AI effects. The abstract does not establish the full response counts, question wording, calibration error, policy implementation, or whether forecasts change behavior.
observations.subgroup: Academic economists, AI-company employees, AI policy researchers, highly accurate forecasters, and the general public; workers and households appear as forecasted populations rather than linked outcomes.
observations.counterinterpretation: Forecast disagreement can reflect informed uncertainty rather than ideology, and policy preferences may respond to values or distributional concerns unrelated to the numerical forecast; rapid-progress assumptions may not occur.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI record for the working paper.
Official working-paper PDF for survey and forecast details.

boundary: This record measures expectations, disagreement, and policy preferences about AI under stated scenarios. It does not establish realized productivity, employment, labor-force participation, GDP, retraining, job-guarantee, UBI, household welfare, or political action.
